_README: Every money figure DK 2015 gives, plus the structural money rules the book states. ALL figures are 2015 leads and may never be printed (project hard rule 1; corrections.json #1 forbids ATM fee/cap figures outright). The usable part of each entry is the STRUCTURE (what is cheap relative to what, what is negotiable, what gets taxed), not the number. costTiers in site config stays empty until a current verified range exists.

structural_rules.claim: Tourist-zone shops quoted in US dollars because it earned them more; paying in dong was cheaper. Dong is the only legal tender.
structural_rules.verify_against: State Bank of Vietnam rules on foreign-currency pricing (quoting in USD is now restricted); practice on the ground

structural_rules.claim: In 2015 USD was accepted almost everywhere, notes had to be in mint condition, and small dong notes were advised for daily spending.
structural_rules.verify_against: Today USD acceptance is far narrower; mint-note rule still true at exchange counters

structural_rules.claim: Dong cannot be changed back outside Vietnam; spend or convert before leaving.
ATMs dispense dong only, with a per-withdrawal cap and a per-withdrawal flat fee; unlimited withdrawals per day; larger sums over the counter.
structural_rules.conflict_with: corrections.json #1: the book gives a cap (2–5 million dong) and fee (US$2–5) — those figures must NOT be printed; only the structural rule (flat fee + low cap → withdraw the maximum, rarely) is publishable

structural_rules.claim: Banks are slow, private exchanges faster at worse rates, gold/jewellery shops give the best rates but no recourse on short-changing or counterfeits; most travellers just use ATMs.
structural_rules.verify_against: Legality of gold-shop exchange (technically unlicensed); Ha Trung street in Hanoi practice

structural_rules.claim: Visa/Mastercard work at airlines, agencies, upmarket hotels, restaurants and tourist shops in the big cities; not in small towns, markets, bus stations or street food; cash advances at banks.
Notes 500 to 500,000 dong, all with Ho Chi Minh's face; 10,000 and up are polymer; coins (2004) were widely refused.
structural_rules.verify_against: Coins no longer circulate; sub-1,000 notes effectively gone
structural_rules.note: The 20,000 vs 500,000 polymer-blue lookalike trap is NOT in the book but belongs in our money article.

structural_rules.claim: High-end hotels add 10% VAT plus 5% service, shown on the bill; budget places bundle it.
structural_rules.verify_against: VAT rate (temporarily 8% in 2024–25 stimulus); hotel practice

structural_rules.claim: Walk-in hotel rates were negotiable, up to ~30% off at big hotels for week-long stays or lesser rooms; budget places only a few dollars.
structural_rules.verify_against: OTA-era pricing makes walk-in discounts rarer

structural_rules.claim: Outside malls and chains the first price is double or more the settle price, except food and drink; bargain with humour, patience and the walk-away.
A foreigner/local two-tier price (up to 5x) was 'officially abolished but still prevalent', especially at government-owned hotels and some sights.
structural_rules.verify_against: Current ticket boards at Hue, Hoi An, My Son (single price); residual dual pricing at some provincial sites

structural_rules.claim: All sales final; electronics may carry a replacement guarantee, not a refund.

LP 2016: the dong is the currency but USD was 'widely used', less so rurally; businesses quote in whichever they prefer; tatty big USD bills are refused; you cannot legally take dong out of the country but can reconvert reasonable amounts to USD on departure; land borders now have official exchange.
structural_rules.verify_against: State Bank rules on foreign-currency pricing; today dong-only is the norm

structural_rules.claim: ATMs in virtually every town; Maestro/Cirrus, Visa and Mastercard all work; each withdrawal carries a flat fee and a per-transaction cap that varies by bank (LP names banks with higher caps).
structural_rules.conflict_with: corrections.json #1: the structural rule is publishable, the fee and cap figures are not

structural_rules.claim: Visa and Mastercard accepted in major cities and tourist centres but not at budget guesthouses or noodle bars; a surcharge of around 3% is sometimes added; cash advances at Vietcombank for 3%+ commission.

Bargaining is essential in most tourist transactions but must be good-natured because face matters; sometimes 50% off, sometimes 10%; once money is accepted the deal is done. Hotels discount if asked; restaurants are fixed; some bus drivers overcharge foreigners.
Top-end hotels add 10% tax and 5% service shown as '++' on the bill; some midrange and even budget places try to add 10% 'though this can often be waived'.
structural_rules.verify_against: Current VAT rate and hotel practice

structural_rules.claim: The dong had been stable at around 22,000 to the dollar for several years (2016).
There is no real black market in currency; gold shops and exchange counters are the informal channels.
Traveller's cheques are 'a total pain to cash' — few banks touch them.
Refuse ripped or torn dong notes, especially VND 10,000 and up — shops reject them and you are stuck; ask any exchange counter to swap worn notes.
Exchange kiosks are usually not bank-affiliated but are safe because counterfeit dong is not a significant problem; gold shops and hotels also exchange at varying rates.
Banks keep office hours (foreign banks 8–5, domestic often closing 4–4:30) and almost all break for lunch from about 11 to 1:30; some open Saturday mornings.
Moon 2015: domestic ATM fees minimal, foreign-bank machines rarely over VND 10,000 per withdrawal.
structural_rules.conflict_with: corrections.json #1 — fees and caps are not publishable; today's foreign-card fees are several times this

structural_rules.claim: Ask the price before eating street-side: doubling or tripling the bill at the end is the known trick; agreeing first removes it. Tourist-heavy places (Phu Quoc, Hoi An) cost more; the Delta and Central Highlands a fraction.
A restaurant meal can cost ten times a street meal; what you pay for is atmosphere — the food at the hole-in-the-wall is often as good or better.
Moon's bargaining heuristic: survey a few vendors, then offer 20–40% below the going ask; never start haggling unless you intend to buy — bargaining for sport angers vendors.
Postcards are cheap and take 2–3 weeks; parcels abroad are expensive and may never arrive — ship purchases by courier, not the post.
structural_rules.note: Relevant to decision gap #34 (ship vs carry).

tipping.claim: No tip needed where a service charge exists; US$1 for exceptional help was 'considered generous' in 2015.
Tipping became common with tourism; ~10% in better restaurants and backpacker areas if service is good, nothing if poor; upscale places add 5% service, a small extra is optional.

LP's First Time page: hotels not expected (small gratuity for cleaners optional); restaurants not expected, 5–10% in smart places or if very satisfied, 'locals don't tip'; guides a few dollars per day trip; taxis not necessary, a little extra appreciated at night; bars never.
tipping.conflict_with: DK 2015 p243 '10% appreciated in better restaurants'; no primary source exists (disputes.md tipping_norm). Publish the structural rule: not expected, appreciated, scaled to local wages.

tipping.claim: LP's Directory page frames it differently: 'not expected but enormously appreciated' — a dollar is significant to someone earning US$150 a month; the 5% service charge at upmarket places 'may not make it to the staff'; tip drivers and guides, and tour groups pool a communal tip; a small pagoda donation (about US$2) is proper, especially if a monk showed you round.

Moon, the FOURTH opinion: tipping is neither required nor customary outside high-end restaurants; some places add a service charge; the one real exception is spas and massage, where a tip is expected and a gratuity form may appear; elsewhere whatever you like, and in a country where a dollar buys a meal any tip is appreciated.
tipping.conflict_with: DK p235/p243, LP p21/p482 — four book positions and no primary source (disputes.md tipping_norm); publish the structural rule only

figures_2015._note: Never print. Kept for trend reference only.

accommodation.claim: Basic city room with TV and A/C from ~US$15; small towns US$8–10.
Mid-range US$40–70; luxury from US$100; above US$100 ≈ Western 4–5 star.
Guesthouse/budget hotel US$8 (Dalat) to US$25 (HCMC), average US$10–15; fan room without window ~US$6; dorm bed ~US$5.

food.claim: A full hotel meal under US$15/head; imported wine taxed heavily, spirits less so, local beer cheap; street-food budget traveller ~US$6/day.

transport.claim: Average return fare from the US West Coast ~US$1,500 in 2015; peak Dec–Feb.
Domestic fares usually under US$150 ex-baggage.
Train fares from a few dollars to over US$100.
Bus HCMC–Hanoi US$45–60.
Car + driver US$65–120/day.
xe om ~US 70c/km; full-day hire from ~US$10.
SGN ~US$15, HAN ~US$17, DAD ~US$2 into town.
Taxi meters start just under US$1.

services.claim: Museum/zoo entry typically US$1 or less in 2015; pagodas free with a donation box.
services.verify_against: Hue citadel, Hoi An old-town ticket, My Son, Cu Chi current prices — all far above this now

services.claim: Visa-on-arrival stamping fee US$45 at the airport on top of the agency fee.
services.conflict_with: facts.json visa.fee: e-visa US$25 single / US$50 multiple; VOA letters no longer apply to tourists

services.claim: Postcard to the US about half a dollar; letters 10–14 days; parcels months because of inspection.
Attended pay toilets in central HCMC ~US 10c.
Hoi An tailors copy an outfit in hours at about a third of the home price.

figures_2016._note: Lonely Planet 2016 figures. Never print. Trend reference only.

daily_budgets.claim: LP 2016 daily budgets: budget under US$40 (bia hoi from about 50c, an hour on a local bus US$1–1.50, cheap hotel US$10–15, noodle meal US$1.50–2.50); midrange US$40–100 (comfortable double US$25–50, smart meal from US$8, hour massage US$6–20, ten-minute taxi US$4); top end over US$100 (luxury room from US$80, gourmet meal from US$20, internal flight US$30–100).
Sleeping price bands 2016 (double, high season): under US$25 / US$25–75 / over US$75. Budget rooms of US$12–16 came with wifi, A/C, hot water and TV.
Eating price bands 2016 per meal: under US$5 / US$5–15 / over US$15.

transport.claim: HCMC–Hanoi open-tour through-ticket US$30–75 (2016); rural bus benchmark about US$2–3 per 100 km.

HCMC 2016 fares: to Dalat air from US$41 / bus US$11–15; Nha Trang air from US$22 / bus US$10–20 / train US$14–32; Hue air from US$48 / bus US$26–37 / train US$17–44; Hanoi air from US$62 / bus US$39–49 / train US$47–69.
From Hanoi 2016: Hue ~374k hard seat to ~894k soft sleeper; Danang ~430k–954k; Nha Trang ~692k–1.65m; HCMC ~790k–1.69m dong.
Car with driver US$80–120/day, 4WD US$120–135 (2016).
Semi-auto US$5–7, automatic US$6–10, trail bike US$20+ per day; HCMC Pham Ngu Lao US$10–12; local driver-guide ~US$20/day; guided tours from ~US$100/person/day (2016).
Bicycle US$1–3/day, better models from US$6, mountain bikes US$6–15 (2016).
Hanoi taxi flagfall ~20k then ~15k/km; HCMC flagfall ~12k, Dong Khoi→Pham Ngu Lao ~25k; xe om 15–30k short rides; cyclo 10–40k, ~40–70k/hour; Hanoi electric buggy 250k/hour per buggy (2016).
HCMC airport taxi ~160–190k dong + access fee, bus 6k; Hanoi airport taxi ~400k / US$20, bus 5k, airline shuttles 30–50k (2016).
HCMC–Phnom Penh bus ~230k dong, ~6 h; HCMC–Siem Reap ~450k, ~12 h; Cambodian visa on arrival US$30 (2016).
Unleaded about 20,500 dong per litre (2016).

activities.claim: Two fun dives US$70–80 (Con Dao ~US$160); snorkel day trips US$25–40; PADI Open Water US$325–500 (2016).
Two-hour beginner kitesurf lesson from about US$100 in Mui Ne (2016).
Dalat rafting day trip from US$67 (2016).
A decent imported motorbike helmet from about US$30 in the big cities (2016).

connectivity.claim: SMS 500–2,500 dong, international calls 3–6k/min, 3G 1 GB from 50,000 dong, a basic handset ~300k with credit; mobile international calls from ~US$0.15/min (2016).
Internet cafés 3–8k dong per hour (2016) — effectively extinct.

work.claim: English teaching paid US$10–18/hour at language centres and US$15–25 for home tutoring in 2016, more in HCMC/Hanoi.

figures_2015_moon._note: Moon 2015 figures. Never print. Trend reference only; see figures_2015 (DK) and figures_2016 (LP) for the same years.

arrival.claim: US round trips about US$1,000 ±100–200 in 2015; four figures from the East Coast and interior.

Embassy visa US$100 (1-month single) to US$180 (3-month multiple); agency extension about US$30 against an official US$10; approval-letter route: letter US$15–30 plus airport stamping US$45–95, all cash USD.

transport.claim: Hanoi airport taxi 'no more than' VND 400k, hotel pickup from 350k, VNA minibus 40k, bus 17 5k (2015).
HCMC airport taxi VND 150–180k, xe om to Pham Ngu Lao ≤80k, bus 152 5k (2015).
Taxi flagfall VND 10–15k; Old Quarter xe om ≤40k; cyclo hour from ~100k; city bus 5–7k; Dong Xuan electric car 150k/35 min or 250k/hour per 7-seat car (2015).
Motorbike rental VND 80–200k/day nationally; Hanoi Vietnamese shops ~100k vs foreign-owned ~210k; HCMC Pham Ngu Lao 100–120k (2015).
Mass-market day tours from about VND 100k; Vietjet sale fares as low as VND 100k (2015).
The only decent road atlas cost about VND 300k in bookshops (2015) — Google Maps has made it moot.

daily_life.claim: Street meal VND 15–20k vs restaurant up to 200k; bia hoi ~VND 4k a glass; laundry 25k/kg street vs 35k via hotel (2015).
Cu Chi VND 90k; Perfume Pagoda 50k plus boat; Cat Cat 40k; Hon Chong 5k (2015).
Son Doong expedition about US$3,000 per person (2015).
About VND 21,000 to the dollar; businesses using 20–22k (2015).
Legitimate ESL jobs need a bachelor's, TESOL/CELTA, police check and medical; notarise the degree at home first (2015).
